facts.claim: "Planet TD1" is track 5 on the self-titled debut album Trip The Witch, released 10 September 2021, and runs 4:56.
Trip The Witch is a collaborative project between Stone Temple Pilots guitarist Dean DeLeo and Nashville session guitarist Tom Bukovac.
Tom Bukovac and Dean DeLeo are the credited songwriters of "Planet TD1".

Bandcamp credits for the track: Tom Bukovac (electric guitar, vibes, keyboards), Dean DeLeo (electric guitar, keyboards), Ryan Williams (B3 organ), Steve Mackey (bass) and Ian Fitchuk (drums). Session Days lists Fitchuk on drums and Williams on Hammond organ, but does not list Mackey on this track.

The album was produced by Trip The Witch, mixed by Ryan Williams, and mastered by JJ Golden at Golden Mastering. Engineers were Ryan Williams, Shannon Forrest, Konrad Snyder, Mills Logan and Paul Moak.
Bukovac said "Planet TD1" was one of the first songs the pair came up with, and that it set the template for the album. He said the title stands for 'Tom Dean 1'.
The album was written and recorded entirely online during the pandemic, with the pair emailing parts to each other. DeLeo and Bukovac had not met in person.
Bukovac described the writing process as sending DeLeo a riff and getting one back. After a while they had a million riffs and began assembling them into songs.
The album is ten mostly instrumental tracks. Its first single, "Saturn We Miss You", features vocals by Jon Anderson of Yes.
A remastered edition with 2 bonus tracks was released on 11 January 2022, and it includes a remastered "Planet TD1".

research.lineage: A pandemic-era, remotely recorded guitar-driven instrumental collaboration between a Stone Temple Pilots guitarist and a Nashville session player, tagged by Bandcamp as space rock and instrumental rock.

draft:
A melody arrives on a fast, clean attack, hangs in the air on a long release, then disappears and leaves the rest of the band holding the floor. A pad stretches sustained chords wide. A bass line sits low and patient. Kick and snare keep a steady, driving pulse at a slow walk. Then the melody comes back. **Planet TD1** is built on that small drama of leaving and returning, and it turns out to be the right shape for a song made by two people who had never been in the same room.

Trip the Witch is Dean DeLeo, the Stone Temple Pilots guitarist, and Tom Bukovac, a Nashville session guitarist. They wrote and recorded their self-titled debut entirely online during the pandemic, emailing parts back and forth without ever meeting in person. Bukovac has described the process as sending DeLeo a riff and getting one back, until they had a million riffs and started stitching them into songs. "Planet TD1" was one of the first. The title, he said, stands for "Tom Dean 1," and the track set the template for everything else on the record.

Knowing that changes how the song lands. The feeling here isn't loneliness, exactly. It's closer to the steadiness of a conversation carried on at a distance, where each answer takes a while to arrive and you trust that it will. The rhythm section never wavers. The lead line steps away and the ground holds. When it returns, it doesn't strain or show off. It just picks the thread back up.

The production is polished and smooth, with a long reverb tail that makes the room feel bigger than any one studio. That fits the space-rock and instrumental-rock lineage the record sits in, though this is the calm end of that tradition, closer to drifting than to launching. Both players are credited on electric guitar and keyboards, with Bukovac adding vibes, Ryan Williams on B3 organ, and Ian Fitchuk on drums. Williams also mixed the album. The album's first single brought in Jon Anderson of Yes on vocals, but most of the record, this track included, lets the instruments carry everything.

The song's restraint is its strength. Nothing piles up and nothing breaks loose. The parts repeat and trade places, and the slow, unhurried groove asks you to stay inside it rather than wait for a payoff.

What sticks is that returning melody, which plays like a message answered across a long distance and leaves you feeling that the gap between two people can be crossed if someone keeps sending the next part.
